question: Where else in the solar system has NASA looked for water and ice, and what did each mission actually find?

sub_questions: Which other solar system bodies did NASA missions search for water or ice (Moon, Mars, Mercury, icy moons, dwarf planets, comets, asteroids)?

Which specific NASA missions visited each body and what did each mission actually detect or measure (surface ice, subsurface ice, water vapor plumes, hydrated minerals, evidence of past liquid water)?
What form of water or ice was reported for each finding (exposed surface ice, buried ice, vapor plumes, hydrated minerals, salty deposits) and how did the picture change over time?
phrasings: Where else in the solar system has NASA looked for water and ice, and what did each mission actually find?
The twin Mars rovers were sent to look for evidence of past water on the Martian surface.
The Phoenix lander uncovered and documented water ice in the Martian soil at its polar landing site.
LRO mapping and the LCROSS impact confirmed the presence of water ice in permanently shadowed lunar craters.
MESSENGER mapped radar‑bright deposits at Mercury's poles that were interpreted as water ice in permanently shadowed regions.
Galileo observations indicated a subsurface ocean on Europa and surface features formed in water‑ice.
Cassini discovered active water‑ice plumes venting from Enceladus' south polar region.
Dawn observed bright spots on Ceres and found evidence consistent with buried water ice and briny deposits.
visual_phrasings: Two rovers traversing dusty Martian plains with close‑ups of layered sedimentary rocks and Phoenix arm scooping soil with a patch of bright exposed ice.
High‑contrast images of permanently shadowed lunar polar craters and the LCROSS impact plume, and radar/thermal maps of polar bright deposits on Mercury.
Flyby/facing shots of Europa's fractured icy crust and of Enceladus with narrow jets of material streaming from its south polar fissures; Dawn imagery of Ceres' bright spots.
plan.rationale: I broke the request into (1) which bodies were searched, (2) which NASA missions visited each and the concrete detections they reported, and (3) the form of water/ice and how findings evolved over time so archive narration and visuals can be matched to specific mission results.

answer.answer: NASA has searched for water and ice on the Moon by targeting permanently shadowed polar craters and using the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter’s LEND neutron detector to look for hydrogen (a proxy for water) in the lunar soil [1]. NASA has also searched across Mars with orbiters, early imaging missions and surface rovers—efforts described from Mariner 4 through the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and the twin rovers to modern rovers—to map landing sites and hunt for signs of water [2][4][5]. Those Mars missions have produced direct evidence of past liquid water and wet environments: Curiosity has found lake deposits and other clues to a watery past, Perseverance is studying ancient river-channel sediments (using cameras, geochemistry instruments and subsurface radar), and infrared observations have mapped water-related signatures in the atmosphere [8][7][6]. Together these clips show NASA pursuing both trapped polar hydrogen on an airless body and past-surface/subsurface water on an active planet, using complementary methods (neutron detection from orbit, in‑situ rock investigation, and subsurface radar) to search for hydrogen, hydrated minerals and sedimentary evidence [1][5][7].

chronology.claim: The archive shows that since the 1960s scientists suspected frozen water at the Moon's poles and developed orbital neutron-detection approaches to look for hydrogen in lunar soil [1].

answer.caveats: The clips document searches and findings on the Moon and Mars but do not by themselves prove a definitive detection of surface ice at the lunar poles or provide a complete catalog of all results on Mars; some era labels in the evidence are taken from video or published metadata rather than primary mission dating (e.g., 'scene' or 'video' or 'published' era tags).

evidence.title: Water on the Moon
evidence.spoken: Since the 1960s, scientists have suspected that frozen water could survive in permanently shadowed craters at the Moon's poles. Both hydrogen and oxygen could be trapped within the lunar soil. So to find water on the Moon, scientists are looking for indications of hydrogen using the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's LEND neutron Detector. By observing the interaction of neutrons with the lunar soil, scientists can interpret how much hydrogen is likely to be present. In order to make a detailed interpretation, however, LEND needs to observe a large number of neutrons. Because LRO is constantly moving, LEND is never over one place long enough to count many neutrons. So to make a detailed interpretation of neutron flux, scientists add together many measurements from many orbits.

evidence.text: A stitched panoramic view of a dusty, reddish rock outcrop and sandy plain on Mars with clear rover wheel tracks across rippled sand. The lower-right corner of the main image shows part of the rover (wheel, suspension/arm and a shadow) indicating the scene is taken from a rover-mounted camera. Foreground contains small fractured rocks, layered bedrock slabs, and sand dunes; midground shows a steep layered rock scarp with cross-bedding and small talus. Overlaid title cards and cutaways appear: a large white-on-black label reading 'BONANZA KING', a close-up of a rounded, pale rock, and a collage including terrestrial photos of dunes and a map outline of California with '118°' and 'Area of map' called out, linking the Mars target name to an Earth analog (Death Valley/Bonanza King). No mission clocks or numeric data readouts are visible in the frames. The frames show both an overhead, color-enhanced orbital view and close-up rover surface panoramas of a layered outcrop area. The top images are a false-color / enhanced satellite view of an elongate, light-toned linear ridge (referred to in the speech as the “Bacon Strip”) sitting at the base of a steeper, darker scarp; small circular pits and streaked sand/ripple patterns are visible immediately downslope from the ridge. The lower frames are ground-level Mastcam-style images showing the rover’s hardware at the lower-left edge and a foreground of broken, light-toned fractured bedrock plates, scattered angular rock slabs, and dark fine sand drifts leading up to tilted, multi-layered outcrops on a slope. Overall the scene documents sedimentary layering, thin light-toned deposits, talus and aeolian sand sorting, combining orbital overview imagery with rover surface photos while the narrator mentions the Perseverance arrival and informal feature naming. A stitched color panorama of a Martian ground site fills the frame: light-toned, fractured bedrock and angular rock chips cover the foreground, with finer sand and small ripples between clasts. Mid- to background show layered, slabby outcrops and a steep talus slope rising to a rim. Part of rover hardware is visible at the lower-left edge of the image. A large, bold white text label 'HOGWALLOW FLATS' is overlaid across the lower middle of the panorama, and a small burned-in caption in the upper corner reads 'PERSEVERANCE JEZERO CRATER, MARS · 18 FEB 2021.' The cutaways in the same segment show two people in an indoor interview set (one wearing a Perseverance mission t‑shirt) and archival photos of a National Park ranger at Mount Rainier, but the primary scientific imagery shown is the Perseverance surface panorama of layered Martian rocks and regolith.
evidence.title: How Does NASA Name Things on Mars? (Mars Report - June 2023)
evidence.spoken: One of my favorite Curiosity targets is called Bonanza King, which is named after the Bonanza King Rock Formation near Death Valley. Here we see an area that resembles a strip of bacon when viewed from space, so we jokingly called it the Bacon Strip. Since arriving at the site with Perseverance, we had to give it a name that fit the Shenandoah theme, so we chose Hog Wallow Flats. If you could come up with a name for a rock, what would it be? I spent seven summers as the Night Skies ranger at Mount Rainier national park, so I'd probably pick something named after Mount Rainier or a place that's special to me inside the park.

evidence.title: KSC-05-S-00033
evidence.spoken: This July will mark the two year anniversary of the launch of the twin Mars exploration Rovers Spirit and Opportunity. Since Mars passes close to Earth every 26 months, that means it's almost time for NASA to launch a new mission to the red planet the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Set to launch in August, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter will build on the discoveries and advances of recent successful Mars missions. The orbiter will call upon its suite of innovative scientific instruments to study the atmosphere, terrain and even what lies below the planet's surface. The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter will snap photos of selected targets on Mars rough surface in more detail than any previous orbiter, revealing features as small as a coffee table. The mission will allow scientists on Earth to study Martian terrain too dangerous to visit.

evidence.title: KSC-04-S-00404
evidence.spoken: Before long, Spirit was covering up to 360ft a day and shattering distance records along the way. The rover's initial work site was a rock dubbed Adirondack. Using its grinding tool, Spirit became the first robot ever to carve into Martian rock. From there, the rover ventured to other sites, like Humphrey Ebenezer and into the Columbia Hills. It was in the Columbia Hills that Strike Spirit finally hit the geological jackpot and found the mineral hematite. Hematite often forms in water, water that may have nurtured life on Mars.

evidence.title: Mars' Ancient Ocean
evidence.spoken: And how did it lose that water? To answer this question, a team of researchers at NASA's Goddard Space Flight center used infrared telescopes on Earth to study water molecules in the Martian atmosphere. We used the world's three major telescopes for infrared astronomy. From the ground, we could actually take a snapshot of the whole hemisphere of the planet on a single night. The new infrared maps reveal the atmospheric ratio of normal to heavy water molecules at different locations and seasons. On Mars, heavy water molecules contain a heavy isotope of hydrogen called deuterium, which remains trapped in the Martian water cycle while normal hydrogen is lost to space. The researchers found that water from the polar ice caps is highly enriched in deuterium, indicating that Mars has lost a tremendous quantity of water.

evidence.title: Perseverance Explores Ancient River Channel (Mars Report)
evidence.spoken: Before we get to the rim, though, we're making a stop at a site called Bright Angel. The rocks there could contain sediments deposited by one of the last bursts of water into the crater and could be amongst the youngest rocks we've looked at yet. Perseverance is equipped with cameras, geochemistry instruments, and an underground underground radar. We're going to use observations from these instruments to determine how and when these rocks formed. And depending on what we find, we may decide to sample these rocks. Whether Bright angel is older or younger than what we've seen before in the crater, these rocks could be an important bookend to our Jezero sample collection.

evidence.title: NASA’s Curiosity Rover Finds New Clues to Mars’ Watery Past
evidence.spoken: Foreign. The Curiosity rover has discovered lots of evidence of ancient lakes on Mars. But what we saw in this panorama surprised us. Curiosity is currently exploring Mount Sharp. You can see the upper part of the mountain here. The Whole Mountain is 3 miles tall, but we're down in the foothills. In 2022, the rover started exploring a unique feature on Mars called the Marker band. It's a dark, thin layer of rock that stands out from the layers above and below it. We first saw it in orbiter images years before we launched.
